Event-driven control of hybrid systems using
Batches Petri nets: Application to high throughput
manufacturing systems
Ruotian Liu, Member, IEEE, Rabah Ammour, Member, IEEE, Leonardo Brenner, and Isabel Demongodin
Abstract—The problem considered in this work concerns the
control of hybrid systems, studied from the discrete event systems
theory viewpoint. The objective is to compute a transient control
trajectory for reaching a steady state from a given initial state.
The hybrid systems are modeled by a class of hybrid Petri nets
called controlled generalized batches Petri nets, which introduce
variable delays on continuous flows for modeling and analysis
of dynamical systems. The key contributions of this study are
as follows: two event-driven control strategies are proposed for
reaching a target steady state, offering advantages in terms
of control actions and time performance. These strategies are
based on ON/OFF state transitions, with the firing flow either
limited to its steady flow or maximal flow; two algorithms are
presented to implement these control strategies effectively; a
case study of a bottling production line, a high throughput
manufacturing system, is provided, demonstrating the application
of the proposed methods and evaluating their efficiency in terms
of time performance and the number of generated events.
Note to Practitioners- In this work, two event-driven control
strategies for reaching a steady state from a given initial
state are presented. We use controlled generalized batches
Petri nets that are suitable discrete event formalism for the
modeling of complex systems such as transportation sys-
tems, high throughput production lines and, crowds behavior.
This Petri net could model groups of moving entities with
given forms (speed, density, length), which allows to consider
variable delays of transfer elements due to congestion or
groups merging. The objective is to reach a target steady state
characterized by constant flows and also particular forms of the
entities groups. This is a challenging issue because the existing
formalisms and methods usually allow to reach a given steady
setting without considering the forms of the entities groups.
The proposed control strategies could be used, for example,
during a recovery mode in order to reach the steady state
after a system’s shutdown, failure or malicious attack. Their
effectiveness is shown on the Perrier mineral water bottling
production line.
Index Terms—Hybrid system, batches Petri net, event-driven
control, steady state.

I. INTRODUCTION
T
echnological advances have increasingly required novel
methodologies for controlling complex dynamical sys-
tems. For hybrid systems, the control problem has attracted
much attention, mainly concerning the aspects on supervisory
control and optimal control to ensure desired system’s behav-
ior [1], [2]. Part of the discrete event systems (DESs) theory,
the objective of this work is, starting from a given initial
state of the hybrid system, to compute a control trajectory
for reaching a given target (steady) state. This is done using
a purely event-driven dynamics [3], [4] in which the control
action is only updated when specific events are triggered.
In DESs theory, Petri net (PN) model arises naturally in
the context of modeling, analysis and synthesis of hybrid
systems abstracted to a discrete event setting [5], [6]. By using
the fluidization technique, continuous Petri nets and hybrid
Petri nets (HPNs) [7], [8] were introduced to avoid the state
space explosion problem and model more accurately those
hybrid systems composed of discrete and continuous parts.
Particularly, a continuous place is used to model pure flow
dynamics in physical systems, such as the continuous variation
of liquid levels in tanks, for instance. Different aspects have
been investigated in continuous Petri nets, including steady
state control [9], structural controllability [10], scheduling
problem [11]. A family of extended HPNs has also been

proposed, such as first-order hybrid Petri nets [12], [13], and
differential Petri nets [14]. However, many man-made systems
contain continuous transfer elements that introduce variable
delays depending on the traffic intensity. These elements
cannot be represented in detail by standard continuous or HPN
models. This motivates the definition of generalized batches
Petri nets (GBPNs) [15] that enrich the class of HPNs by
introducing a new kind of nodes, called batch nodes. Batch
transitions act as continuous ones with finite server semantics
while batch places are hybrid ones defined by three continuous
characteristics: a length, a transfer speed and a maximal
density. In practice, a batch place can model a transfer element
in physical systems, such as a conveyor belt in manufacturing
systems or road section in transportation systems. Based on the
concept of batches as marking, i.e., a group of entities moving
through a batch place at a certain speed, GBPNs allow variable
delays on continuous flows to be represented. Enabling the
study of the phenomena of accumulation or congestion of
entities, they have proven to be powerful formalisms for
describing high throughput production lines and conveyor belts
[16], [17], railway interlocking systems [18], transportation
networks [19], [20] or, transmission delay on a communication
media with bus topology [21]. When the firing flows of
continuous and batch transitions and the transfer speeds of
batch places are considered as control inputs, this defines the
controlled GBPNs (cGBPNs) [22]. Behavior of such hybrid
models is based on a switching continuous-time and event-
driven dynamics. One problem in such dynamical controlled
hybrid systems is determining a stationary state, which can be
maintained for an indefinite time. In a cGBPN without discrete
nodes, this stationary state has been defined as a steady state
where the markings of places and the instantaneous firing
flows of transitions remain constant [22]. The existence and
determination of a steady state has been proposed in [23]
for cGBPN. In this paper, we consider the same settings by
assuming a cGBPN without discrete nodes and, investigate the
control problem to reach such a steady state.
In the literature, recent works investigate different control
approaches in hybrid systems modeled by HPNs. In [24], col-
ored HPNs have been used to model multimodal transportation
systems for achieving an optimal control regarding just-in-
time criterion. In [25], a controlled HPN is used to model
the physical part of an energy router considered as a cyber
physical systems for energy management processes. With the
aim of driving a system to a target state, several works have
addressed the control problem of DESs using timed continuous
and hybrid PNs. They consider external control actions that
consist in slowing down the firing flow of transitions leading
to admissible control laws. These existing approaches in timed
continuous and hybrid PNs can be described according to their
dynamics, i.e., time-driven or event-driven. In terms of time-
driven approach, a control action is updated at each sampling
time. Specifically, a model predictive control approach is
proposed in [26], [27] for reaching a steady state while
optimizing a given quadratic performance index with respect
to markings and controlled firing flow variables. Then an
optimal control action is computed over a future horizon
at each time step. In [28] the desired stationary marking
vector and the desired asymptotic firing rate vector have been
reached by considering the feedback control strategy. In [29],
[30], ON/OFF controllers based on the firing quantity vector
are proposed in controlled timed continuous PNs. The main
advantage of this proposed ON/OFF controller is its low
computational complexity. In terms of event-driven approach,
a control action is updated at each occurrence of specific
events. The study in [31] proposes an event-driven optimal
control in continuous Petri nets, which is further extended to
hybrid Petri net in [32]. Also, the optimal control framework is
improved into a model predictive one, providing a closed-loop
strategy that corrects external disturbances. However, all the
aforementioned methods in terms of both approaches cannot
be directly used in cGBPN. In fact, due to the existence of
batch nodes, in which hybrid dynamics exist inside the batch
places, reaching a steady state consists not only of getting
constant firing flows but also particular forms of the entities
groups (that form the batches).
Inspired by these previous approaches, two different
ON/OFF controllers for cGBPNs are presented in this paper.
Based on the assumptions that the considered cGBPN is
conservative and without discrete nodes, we first propose a
control strategy based on an ON/OFF controller, called steady
flow controller [33]. It assumes that the controlled firing flow
of each transition cannot exceed its steady firing flow. This
is motivated by the phenomenon in many physical systems
where the applied control values are limited by their nominal
values rather than by the maximal values. Moreover, a certain
configuration of the moving entities characterized by a steady
state density should be reached, and the usage of the steady
firing flow allows such configuration to be generated. The
choice of the steady firing flow as a threshold allows one to
construct the regular marking in a batch place. However, this
firing flow limitation implies more delay to reach the steady
state. To improve the time performance of the first proposed
control strategy, a maximal flow controller, is developed [34]
by using the maximal firing flow limitation when a predefined
condition is satisfied, otherwise the steady firing flow limita-
tion is applied. Compared to the steady flow controller, more
events are generated in the maximal flow controller such that
control actions should be frequently updated. Thus, the usage
of two control strategies should achieve a balance between
time performance and control actions. The contributions of
this work can be summarized as follows:
• The control problem for reaching a given steady state
from an initial marking in a cGBPN is formulated, by
considering the instantaneous firing flow of transitions as
control input.
• Two different control strategies have been investigated,
both based on ON/OFF controller, named steady flow
controller and maximal flow controller.
• To validate the proposed control methods, a case study on
a bottling production line, i.e., a high throughput manu-
facturing system, is presented. Moreover, their efficiency
in terms of time performance and the number of generated
events is also analyzed.

Assumption (A2) imposes that each place is contained in the
support of a P-semiflow and, each transition is contained in
the support of a T-semiflow. Assumption (A3) implies that
the considered steady firing flow of each continuous or batch
transition is not null. One way to ensure this assumption is
that the net is consistent (i.e., ∃y > 0 s.t. C · y = 0).
Remark 2: In a practical viewpoint, assumption (A1) im-
plies that, the physical manufacturing system is viewed as
a pure fluid system with variable transfer delay and there
exists no discrete control part. Assumption (A2) shows that
the total weighted value of resources or materials remains
constant. This means that, despite the movement and trans-
formation of materials within the manufacturing system, the
overall weighted value of various resources does not change,
ensuring balanced operations. Assumption (A3) illustrates that,
in a stationary behavior, the high throughput manufacturing
system maintains stable and balanced use of resources, thus
guaranteeing continuous production through the entire system.
IV. TWO CONTROL STRATEGIES FOR REACHING STEADY
STATES
In this section, we mainly present two control methods for
reaching a given reachable steady state from an initial one in
cGBPNs. Two controllers, namely the steady flow controller
and the maximal flow controller, are proposed, in which both
are based on event-driven and ON/OFF control strategies.

V. CASE STUDY
In this section, we study the modeling and control of a
bottling production line system, which is an example of high
throughput manufacturing systems. Due to their high speed
characteristic, a fluid point of view is considered for the
modeling of such systems. In order to characterize the variable
delay on continuous flow and the moving group entities, the
considered system is modeled by a cGBPN. At the beginning
of the production (or after a shutdown due to a failure or a
malicious attack), the system’s current state (represented by the
initial state of the cGBPN model) could be any state different
from the nominal one. In this case, it is necessary to control
the system to reach its nominal operation (represented by a
known steady state of the cGBPN model). To achieve this
goal, the proposed SF-controller and MF-controller are used
to compute the transient trajectory and the simulation results
for each controller are obtained.

empty, the controlled firing flow is reduced from 400 to 200

As a result, compared with the SF-controller, the MF-
controller reaches the steady state more quickly while con-
sidering more events. Specifically, for the unpalletizer and the
washing machine, the MF-controller frequently updates con-
trol actions in the time interval [0, 15.9] (see Fig. 5(a)(b)),with
its controlled flow as the maximal one or zero, similar to bang-

changes control action once at τ = 33.4 for the washing
machine, providing greater stability. For the rotary filler and
packaging machines, compared to the MF-controller, the SF-
controller has a time delay in updating their unique control
action. Consequently, the SF-controller reaches the steady state
with a 15.9 time unit delay relative to the MF-controller. In the
bottling production line system, the SF-controller is preferred
due to its more stable control strategy, which is beneficial for
the operation and longevity of the machines.
Although the proposed approaches in this work cannot
always guarantee the optimality of the obtained transient
control trajectory, considering the unique advantage of both
controllers in terms of event generation and time efficiency,
the selection between the two proposed methods should take
into account the user’s requirements to determine the trade-
off. Note that our proposed control strategies are effective
for the systems studied, scaling them to more complex high-
throughput manufacturing systems may present challenges.
Potential issues include increased computational complexity,
and ensuring real-time responsiveness, which could be miti-
gated by adopting modular control architectures and leveraging
distributed computing resources.

strategies, i.e., steady and maximal flow control laws, have
been proposed as discrete controllers. Algorithms that compute
control trajectory for reaching a given steady state from
an initial marking have been developed. The steady flow
controller assumes that the controlled firing flow of each
transition cannot exceed its steady firing flow, which promotes
the regular forms of batch places to be well constructed.
Instead, the maximal flow controller uses the maximal and
steady firing flow as the limitation of the controlled firing flow
of transitions, in which the two thresholds depend on specific
conditions. Particularly, the maximal flow limitation is used to
approach the steady quantities of places and the steady flow
limitation is used to generate the regular forms of batch places.
Finally, although more events and flow constraints should be
determined at each event time in the algorithm of the MF-
controller, it drives the net to the steady state from an initial
one within less delay compared with the SF-controller. The
cGBPN formalism and the proposed control strategies could
be well used to model and control the application of a bottling
production line.
Future studies would extend the present work to the design
of a minimum time control strategy for reaching a given steady
state, and remove the considered assumptions in this work. In
addition, we will also investigate the control strategy when
both transfer speed of batch places and controlled firing flow
of transitions are considered as control inputs.

Abstract: The problem considered in this work concerns the control of hybrid systems, studied from the discrete event systems theory viewpoint. The objective is to compute a transient control trajectory for reaching a steady state from a given initial state. The hybrid systems are modeled by a class of hybrid Petri nets called controlled generalized batches Petri nets, which introduce variable delays on continuous flows for modeling and analysis of dynamical systems. The key contributions of this study are as follows: two event-driven control strategies are proposed for reaching a target steady state, offering advantages in terms of control actions and time performance. These strategies are based on ON/OFF state transitions, with the firing flow either limited to its steady flow or maximal flow; two algorithms are presented to implement these control strategies effectively; a case study of a bottling production line, a high throughput manufacturing system, is provided, demonstrating the application of the proposed methods and evaluating their efficiency in terms of time performance and the number of generated events. Note to Practitioners- In this work, two event-driven control strategies for reaching a steady state from a given initial state are presented. We use controlled generalized batches Petri nets that are suitable discrete event formalism for the modeling of complex systems such as transportation sys- tems, high throughput production lines and, crowds behavior. This Petri net could model groups of moving entities with given forms (speed, density, length), which allows to consider variable delays of transfer elements due to congestion or groups merging. The objective is to reach a target steady state characterized by constant flows and also particular forms of the entities groups. This is a challenging issue because the existing formalisms and methods usually allow to reach a given steady setting without considering the forms of the entities groups. The proposed control strategies could be used, for example, during a recovery mode in order to reach the steady state after a system’s shutdown, failure or malicious attack. Their effectiveness is shown on the Perrier mineral water bottling production line.
